openingMessage: It takes time to create excellence. If it could be done quickly, more people would do it.
openingWhy: Nobody catches trapped pressure on a 'dead' line in his first month. That catch comes from a thousand honest LMRAs where nothing was wrong. Every real check you run today is buying the instinct that saves you in year five.
leadershipThought: Think before you speak. Think before you joke. Think before you act. Ask yourself: if this shows up in front of a client, my family, or leadership — does it represent me well? If the answer is no — don't do it.

specialFocus.title: Week 23 Starts Here: Same Fight, Heads on a Swivel Through the Holidays
specialFocus.why:
Jacob, this week is yours. Start with the message, then last week straight from Matt Croom's form reviews, then the topic: Operational Discipline through a season full of distractions. Thanksgiving is a week from Thursday, days off are stacking up, and minds start going home before the job is done.

“We're in the same fight together. We all want the best for our families and ourselves. We sacrifice for them, and we need their support too. Stay diligent, keep your head on a swivel, and watch each other's backs.”
— Mike Lyons

Friday showed what that looks like. Bobby Galindo stopped someone from going in without a harness. Robert Henigan stopped a crew using a steel hammer in H2S service. Neither one was about paperwork. They were watching somebody else's back.

✓ LAST WEEK'S GOOD: say these names
  • Bobby Galindo, Emma Jane CTB (Fri): someone was about to go in without a harness or a tag line. Galindo stopped it, and both were in place before anyone entered.
  • Robert Henigan, Hoelscher 2TM (Fri): the crew was using a regular hammer in H2S service. Henigan stopped them until they had a brass one.
  • Jordan Lemmons, Benedum 3A 1H (Sat): found a leaking casing valve, paused the job, and came back only after the valve was changed and holding.
  • Bryan Medlin, XBC Giddings Estate R40 4089H (Fri): gas showed at the first break. Medlin called a hold point, waited until it read zero, and kept monitoring. That's the process working.
  • Nothing to fix all day: Nathan Contreras (Tue), Michael Jobe and Hayden Haugh (Wed), and Justin Pack on both Friday and Saturday.
  • Bobby Fleming (Fri): every photo on the field service form taken that day. Brianda Sandoval: complete bottle entries on the readiness forms Friday and Saturday.
✗ LAST WEEK'S MISSES: these belong to all of us
  • Four real stops, zero ticks. Galindo, Henigan and Lemmons stopped work for real reasons, and Monday's tag line was a stop too. "Stop work authority utilized" was ticked zero times all week. On one of those jobs, the partner's form named the unsafe tool but ticked nothing. If the work stopped, tick utilized on both forms and write two lines.
  • Copied forms. Wednesday, the same "what went well" list was on more than a dozen forms. Saturday, one job's write-up was word-for-word identical to a job at a different well. Every well gets its own form.
  • Trailer forms short every day. Two inspections and the readiness form, every trailer, every day it's out.
  • Old photos. JSA and gas log photos from 2020 were still showing up on job forms. If the photo isn't from today, it proves nothing about today.
  • FRs go where you go. If there's any chance you get sent from the shop to a job, your FRs are on you when you leave.
On the office, not the crew: a trailer went out short an SCBA and with no flags, cones or tape, a rig ran short of mask bags, one contractor's only pair of FRs was in for repair with no spare, and one still reports none issued. Restocking and second sets are on us.
specialFocus.standardLabel: Week 23: Operational Discipline When Your Mind Is Somewhere Else
standard: Leave it at the gate. Before the first break, phone away, and say the job out loud with your partner: what, where, who calls it.
Holiday roads are the most dangerous part of the day. Phone down behind the wheel, heavier traffic, and deer moving at dawn and dusk. Your family wants you home more than they want you home early.
Rest is equipment. Extra shifts to cover days off and long drives home add up. If you're running on empty, tell your lead before the job, not after.
New partner? Brief like it's day one. Holiday coverage puts people on crews they don't usually run with. Don't assume they know how you work.
The last job before days off is where shortcuts happen. The job ends when the work is right and the form is true, not when the truck is pointed home.
Heads on a swivel. If your partner is off today, ask. If something's wrong on location, stop it, and tick utilized.

scenarios.title: The Last Well Before Thanksgiving
scenarios.body: It's the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Last well of the day, a four-hour drive home after it, and your phone has been buzzing all afternoon with family plans. Your partner is quiet and skipped the walk-around on the trailer. The company man wants the line opened so everyone can leave. Nobody is doing anything crazy. That's exactly how it happens. Take thirty seconds: phones away, "you good?" to your partner, say the job back, then break containment. Jacob, ask the circle: what's the one thing you'd skip on that last well, and who would catch it?

questions: What's pulling at your attention this week, and what will you do to leave it at the gate?
How will you know if your partner is off today? What would you say?
Galindo, Henigan and Lemmons all stopped work last week. What would make you stop a job in front of another company's crew?
What does your family do that makes this job possible? Have you told them?
specialFocus.nonNegotiable: Phone down, eyes up, and watch your partner. If something's wrong, stop it and tick "utilized." We all go home for the holidays.
